_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. Before you romanize any name, check here. status per entry: 'attested' (form used in English scholarship / standard romanization, give the basis in note), 'provisional' (romanization mine, not found in outside sources), 'decided' (a project style call). If you find a better attested form mid-book, change it here AND grep every built chapter for the old form, then rebuild. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored. 'pinyin' holds the romaji reading (this is a Japanese book). Flag main cast with "principal": true (+ optional "cast" one-liner, "cast_order") for the Principal Characters page.

土方歳三.cast: The novel's hero. A well-off farmer's son of Ishida village in the Tama country west of Edo, who becomes vice-commander of the Shinsengumi.
土方歳三.note: Historical figure, 1835–1869. Japanese name order, surname (Hijikata) first; the given name Toshizō carries a long final vowel. Called Toshi by his intimates.

近藤勇.cast: Toshizō's boyhood friend and sword-brother, from the neighboring village of Kamiishiwara; commander of the Shinsengumi.
近藤勇.note: Historical figure, 1834–1868. Head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū school of swordsmanship and, later, commander of the Shinsengumi.

佐藤彦五郎.note: Historical, 1827–1902. Headman (nanushi) of Hino, married to Toshizō's elder sister; his household kept the Tennen Rishin-ryū training hall where Kondō and Toshizō trained.

小桜.note: A bell-shaking shrine maiden (miko) at the Ōkunitama Shrine in Fuchū; a minor character. Romanization mine.

お佐絵.note: Younger sister of the Saruwatari chief priest of Fuchū; the woman Toshizō meets in the festival dark. Apparently the novelist's invention. Romanization mine.

猿渡.note: The hereditary house of chief priests (gūji) of the Ōkunitama Shrine at Fuchū, documented from the fourteenth century.

梶川景次.note: A master of the Shintō Munen-ryū with a training hall at Sakuramachi in Kōfu; a minor figure. Reading of the given name uncertain; romanization mine.

六車宗伯.note: A swordsman of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, deputy master at Fuchū, whom Toshizō kills in this chapter. The surname is read Rokusha on the source’s own furigana (ろくしゃそうはく), echoing the Rokusha Myōjin shrine he serves; hence the chapter title, ‘Cutting Down Rokusha.’

瀬木掃部.note: One of the hereditary priestly houses (shake) of the Rokusha Myōjin at Fuchū, in whose residence Rokusha Sōhaku lodged. Romanization mine.

松平伊織.note: A hatamoto of eight hundred koku with a residence in Honjo, Edo; Osae’s late husband, married to her when she was seventeen. A minor figure; reading from the source’s furigana.

近藤内蔵助.note: A rōnin of Enshū, late-eighteenth-century founder of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

近藤周斎.note: Historical. Third head of the Tennen Rishin-ryū (personal name Shūsuke; in retirement, Shūsai), who adopted the farm boy Katsuta and made him Kondō Isami, his heir.

井上源三郎.cast: A steady older man of the Tama circle, from Hino, a Tennen Rishin-ryū fencer who follows Kondō to Kyoto and captains the Shinsengumi's Sixth Unit.
井上源三郎.note: Historical, 1829–1868. One of the founding Tama members of the Shinsengumi; killed at Toba-Fushimi.

永倉新八.cast: A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, a rōnin of Matsumae and one of the corps' great swordsmen; later captain of the Shinsengumi's Second Unit.
永倉新八.note: Historical, 1839–1915. Held the full transmission of the Shintō Munen-ryū; survived the Restoration and left an inside memoir of the corps.

藤堂平助.note: Historical, 1844–1867. A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū; later captain of the Shinsengumi’s Eighth Unit, killed at the Aburanokōji affair after joining Itō Kashitarō’s breakaway.

七里研之助.cast: A fair-skinned iai master with a mark below his right eye, deputy at the Hiruma hall; Toshizō's recurring nemesis, who hunts him for the killing of Rokusha.
七里研之助.note: The chief personal antagonist of the novel's early and middle chapters. An iai master of the Araki-ryū, trained first in the Maniwa Nen-ryū; reading from the source's furigana (しちりけんのすけ).

沖田総司.cast: A boyish prodigy of the Tennen Rishin-ryū, raised at Kondō's Edo hall; the corps's finest swordsman, later captain of the First Unit.
沖田総司.note: Historical, about 1842–1868. Died young of consumption; one of the most beloved figures of the Shinsengumi legend.

お咲.note: A meshimori-onna at the Jōshūya inn in Fuda, a thin-lipped Jōshū woman; a minor figure. Romanization mine.

理兵衛.note: Keeper of the Jōshūya inn at Fuda, the Tennen Rishin-ryū men's regular lodging. Romanization mine.

善海.note: Abbot of the Senjubō, the Shinshū temple in Hachiōji where Toshizō lodged in his peddling days. Romanization mine.

大島新五右衛門.note: An eighteenth-century rural samurai of Kōzuke (died 1779) famous for a trick-drawing feat of the Araki-ryū iai.

半造.note: Son of Hiruma Yohachi and head, from a hall in Senninmachi at Hachiōji, of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū; married to Sen, daughter of the abbot of the Senjubō.

辰吉.note: A young man of Renjaku who peddled horse-sandals at Hachiōji; a passing figure.

石翠.note: Toshizō's eldest brother, blind from birth, who gave up the succession and lived by his arts — a shrewd, polished man. A historical figure (the eldest Hijikata brother); Sekisui is his elegant by-name.

喜六.note: A farmer of Ishida village, Toshizō's eldest surviving brother and head of the house.

千葉栄次郎.note: Historical, 1833–1862. Second son of Chiba Shūsaku and a swordsman prodigy of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū, nicknamed the Little Tengu of Chiba.

周作.note: Founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and of the Genbukan hall in Edo; father of Eijirō. One of the great sword-reformers of the age.

岡田総右衛門.note: Founder of the Ryūgō-ryū of Warabi, the shin-cutting country school.

権.note: An old temple servant of the Shōkōin, once rescued by Toshizō, who serves as his scout. Romanization from the source's furigana.

おのぶ.note: Toshizō's elder sister, wife of Satō Hikogorō.

新田義貞.note: The fourteenth-century commander who, for the emperor Go-Daigo, destroyed the Kamakura shogunate; victor at Bubaigawara in 1333.

三浦義勝.note: A Sagami warrior whose reinforcements turned the Battle of Bubaigawara for Nitta.

真庭十郎左衛門.note: As Shiba gives him, the head of the Nen-ryū house at Maniwa and Chiba Shūsaku's antagonist in the Ikaho affair. The historical head of the Maniwa Nen-ryū was of the Higuchi family; Shiba names him from the school's seat.

深津.note: A pupil of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū, set to make fire during the ambush; a passing figure.

桂小五郎.cast: A Chōshū swordsman, head student of the Renpeikan, blessed in birth, learning, and skill; later, as Kido Takayoshi, an architect of the Meiji Restoration. Toshizō's opposite in every advantage.
桂小五郎.note: Historical, 1833–1877. Later known as Kido Takayoshi, one of the leaders of the Restoration.

原田左之助.cast: A house-guest at the Edo dōjō, a hot-blooded spearman of Iyo; later a captain of the Shinsengumi.
原田左之助.note: Historical, 1840–1868. A spearman of the Hōzōin line; died in the fighting around Edo.

坂本竜馬.note: Historical, 1836–1867. Of Tosa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū swordsman of the Chiba hall; later the great broker of the Restoration, assassinated in 1867.

斎藤弥九郎.note: Master of the Renpeikan, the Shintō Munen-ryū hall reckoned one of the three great dōjō of Edo; Kondō's source of borrowed swordsmen.

桃井春蔵.note: Master of the Shigakukan, one of the three great dōjō of Edo. Reading from the source's furigana (もものい).

塚原卜伝.note: A sword-saint of the sixteenth century.

伊藤一刀斎.note: Founder of the Ittō-ryū line of swordsmanship.

宮本武蔵.note: The famous seventeenth-century duelist, author of The Book of Five Rings.

おつね.note: Kondō Isami's wife, a silent, gloomy woman and, by Toshizō's account, a poor cook.

楠正成.note: The fourteenth-century loyalist commander, byword for cunning generalship against the odds; claimed founder of the Kusunoki school of military science.

武田信玄.note: The sixteenth-century warlord of Kai, whose tactics were handed down as the Kōshū school of military science.

江川.note: The hereditary intendant house at Nirayama, administering shogunal land.

山南敬助.cast: The eldest of the Shieikan house-guests, a learned Sendai man and Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept; brings the corps its political news. Toshizō despises him.
山南敬助.note: Historical, 1833–1865. Held the full transmission at the Chiba hall; later general secretary (sōchō) of the Shinsengumi, second only to Kondō, until an attempt to leave the corps forced him to commit seppuku.

芹沢鴨.cast: A huge, violent Mito rōnin of the Shintō Munen-ryū, of the Tengu Party; co-commander of the founding Mibu corps, and Toshizō's uneasy first ally in Kyoto.
芹沢鴨.note: Historical, 1826/27–1863. A Mito man of the Shindō Munen-ryū, real name given variously as Kimura or Shimomura Tsuguji; first head of the Mibu corps, assassinated by the Kondō faction in the ninth month of 1863.

斎藤一.cast: A close, taciturn swordsman, a rōnin of Akashi who joins the corps from the Shieikan; one of its finest blades.
斎藤一.note: Historical, 1844–1915. Later captain of the Shinsengumi's Third Unit and one of its deadliest swordsmen; survived the wars, served as a Meiji policeman, and died in old age.

清河八郎.note: Historical, 1830–1863. A rural samurai of Shōnai in Dewa, a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and strategist; conceived the Rōshigumi and tried to turn it to the imperial cause, and was cut down for it in 1863.

松平上総介.note: As Shiba gives him: a collateral Tokugawa, of the line of Tadanaga, acting as a sponsor of the rōshi levy. A minor figure; reading of the title as the source gives it.

松平忠敏.note: A Kōbusho instructor placed in charge of the shogunate's rōshi levy of 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (ただとし).

山岡鉄太郎.note: Historical, 1836–1888. A shogunal overseer of the Rōshigumi; later famous as Yamaoka Tesshū, a great swordsman, statesman, and Zen adept who helped negotiate the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

松平容保.note: Historical, 1836–1893. Lord of Aizu and, from 1862, Kyoto Protector (Kyoto Shugoshoku); under his patronage the Mibu corps became the Shinsengumi.

板倉周防守.note: Itakura Katsukiyo (1823–1889), a senior councilor (rōjū) of the shogunate.

新見錦.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early officer of the corps; forced to commit seppuku in 1863. Reading from the source's furigana (にいみにしき).

平間重助.note: A Mito follower and inner pupil of Serizawa Kamo. Romanization mine.

野口健司.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction and an early Shinsengumi officer; died in 1864.

平山五郎.note: A Mito man of the Serizawa faction, killed alongside Serizawa in the assassination of 1863.

石坂周造.note: A defector from Hikone and follower of Kiyokawa; survived into the mid-Meiji years as a man of business, remembered as a pioneer of the Japanese petroleum trade.

池田徳太郎.note: A Geishū (Hiroshima) rōnin of the Kiyokawa faction, active in the levying of the Rōshigumi.

根岸友山.note: A wealthy Musashi headman and expel-the-barbarian sympathizer who enrolled in the Rōshigumi with a following of his own.

八木源之丞.note: A rural samurai of Mibu whose house lodged the corps; the Yagi residence survives as a site of Shinsengumi history.

頼山陽.note: Historical, 1780–1832. Confucian historian and poet, author of the Nihon Gaishi, whose romantic, imperial-centered narrative of Japanese history deeply shaped late-shogunate loyalism.

孝明天皇.note: Reigned 1846–1867. Fiercely opposed to opening the country to foreigners, he lent the loyalist cause an imperial sanction the shogunate could not command.

外島機兵衛.note: A liaison officer (kōyōgata) of the Aizu domain in Kyoto, the corps’s channel to its patron the Kyoto Protector. Reading from the source’s furigana (とじまきへえ).

島津久光.note: Historical, 1817–1887. Father of the young lord of Satsuma and the domain’s effective ruler in these years; it was his procession the English crossed at Namamugi.

佐々木唯三郎.note: Historical, 1833–1868. A shogunal swordsman, later of the Mimawarigumi; killed Kiyokawa Hachirō in 1863 and is widely thought to have led the killing of Sakamoto Ryōma in 1867. Shiba writes the given name 唯三郎; he is also recorded as 只三郎.

谷三十郎.note: Historical, died 1866. Master of the Tōhō Enshin-ryū of spear and sword at Osaka and Harada Sanosuke’s former teacher; later a Shinsengumi captain.

広沢富次郎.note: An Aizu official (later known as Hirosawa Yasuto) who dealt with the Mibu corps at first hand; author of the record the Ōshōroku, quoted here.

九条尚忠.note: Historical, 1798–1871. Head of the Kujō regent house and leader of the pro-shogunate nobles at court; hated by the loyalists, he shaved his head and withdrew after the terror of 1862. Reading from the source’s furigana (ひさただ).

島田左近.note: An agent of the Kujō house and of the shogunal side; cut down in Kiyamachi in the seventh month of 1862 by Satsuma’s Tanaka Shinbei, the first of the loyalist “Heaven’s punishment” killings.

久坂玄瑞.note: Historical, 1840–1864. A leading loyalist of Chōshū, disciple and son-in-law of Yoshida Shōin; died the next year in the Chōshū attack on the Forbidden Gate. Reading from the source’s furigana.

山崎烝.note: Historical, died 1868. Son of an Osaka acupuncturist and the Shinsengumi’s ablest inspector and spy, skilled with the staff; mortally wounded after the sea-fight of Miyako Bay.

赤沢守人.note: A Chōshū man who quit his domain and was taken into the corps as an informer against it; his killing, in 1863, is the case of this chapter. Reading of the given name from the source’s furigana (もりと).

隼人.note: Toshizō’s late father, and also the hereditary given name borne by the head of the Hijikata house.

為三郎.note: Toshizō’s blind eldest brother, who took the poet-name Sekisui the Blind and was passed over for the headship of the house by the law of the day.

三月亭石巴.note: Toshizō’s grandfather, a haiku poet well known in the Hino country in the Bunka–Bunsei years; the source of the family’s haiku tradition.

夏目成美.note: Real haiku poet (1749–1817), a wealthy Asakusa money-changer and a leading master of his day, patron of the young Issa.

松原庵星布.note: Real woman haiku poet (1732–1814) of a notable Hachiōji house; the ni of 星布尼 marks her a lay nun.

家茂.note: Tokugawa Iemochi (1846–1866), the fourteenth Shōgun; a boy still, married to Princess Kazunomiya and made the living token of the union of court and shogunate.

酒井兵庫.note: A veteran jokin of the Shinsengumi, put to death for desertion. See the note in the chapter for the disputed timing.

古高.note: A loyalist agent (1829–1864) who, under the merchant alias Masuya Kiemon, ran an arms depot for the Chōshū-aligned plotters. His arrest set off the Ikedaya raid.

岸淵兵輔.note: A Mito clansman, once a visitor at Kondō’s Edo dōjō, here made the bearer of the first warning about the Masuya. Romanization mine.

四国屋.note: Shōkuōya Jūbei, keeper of the Kiyamachi restaurant Tantora, a known haunt of the Chōshū and Tosa men.

島田魁.note: A Shinsengumi inspector, one of the biggest men in the corps; served on the surveillance of the Masuya.

周平.note: Kondō Shūhei, Kondō Isami’s adopted son, one of the five who charged into the Ikedaya.

渡辺幸右衛門.note: The beat constable who, being on friendly terms with the corps, passed the tip to Mibu rather than to his own office. Romanization mine.

利助.note: A newly hired servant of the Masuya who informed on the arms cache. Romanization mine.

熊坂長範.note: The giant bandit of medieval legend, a stock figure of the theater; see the note in the chapter.

吉田稔麿.note: Chōshū loyalist (1841–1864), a favored pupil of Yoshida Shōin; killed at twenty-four in the Ikedaya fight.

宮部鼎蔵.note: Higo loyalist (1820–1864), a leading strategist of the cause; died at the Ikedaya.

松田重助.note: Higo loyalist, killed at the Ikedaya.

北添佶麿.note: Tosa loyalist, cut down at the head of the Ikedaya stairs. The given name 佶麿 is read Yoshimaro.

望月亀弥太.note: Tosa loyalist, an associate of Sakamoto Ryōma; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly in the street.

野老山.note: Tokoroyama Gokichirō, Tosa loyalist; wounded at the Ikedaya, he cut his belly before the locked Chōshū gate.

大高又次郎.note: Banshū loyalist and leather-armorer; killed at the Ikedaya.

玉虫左大夫.note: A Sendai clansman and diarist (1823–1869); his intelligence-record Kanbu Tsūki preserves these figures. Also written 玉虫左太夫.

惣兵衛.note: Ikedaya Sōbei, keeper of the inn; he died in prison after the affair.

奥沢新三郎.note: The one Shinsengumi corpsman killed outright at the Ikedaya.

安藤早太郎.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

新田革左衛門.note: A Shinsengumi corpsman who died soon after of wounds taken at the Ikedaya.

山田信道.note: Matsuda Jūsuke’s younger brother, later governor of Kyōto Prefecture, who raised the memorial to the Ikedaya dead.

松平定敬.note: Lord of the Kuwana domain in Ise and, from 1864, Kyoto Shoshidai. He was the younger brother of the Kyoto Protector Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the two chief security offices of the capital were thus held by one family.

神保内蔵助.note: An elder councillor (karō) of the Aizu domain and its senior officer on the Kyoto command; full name Jinbō Kuranosuke Toshitaka. He would be made to take his own life in 1868, blamed for the Aizu retreat at Toba-Fushimi.

真木和泉守.note: Maki Izumi (Yasuomi), a Shinto priest of Kurume and the most radical strategist of the loyalist cause; a chief planner of Chōshū's march on Kyoto. He died on Tennōzan (ch. 25).

福原越後.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) who led the Fushimi wing of the 1864 expedition. Wounded in the fighting, he was afterward ordered by his own domain to commit seppuku as one of the three councillors held responsible for the defeat.

来島又兵衛.note: A Chōshū warrior famed for his valor, given command of the Saga (Tenryū-ji) force. He was killed at the Hamaguri Gate (ch. 25).

国司信濃.note: A young Chōshū elder councillor (karō), only twenty-five, given overall field command of the Kyoto expedition. He was ordered to commit seppuku after the defeat.

福田理兵衛.note: A loyalist country samurai (gōshi) of Shimo-Saga who had earlier arranged the billeting of Chōshū troops at the Tenryū-ji. Romanization mine.

武田観柳斎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi, a rōnin of Izumo learned in warrior usage and military science; a flatterer whom Toshizō despised. He was exposed as a Satsuma informer and cut down within the corps in 1867.

蒔田相模守広孝.note: Lord of Bitchū-Asao (ten thousand koku) and commander of the Kyoto Mimawarigumi. (The name is sometimes read Maita; the reading follows the source's own gloss.)

戸田采女正氏彬.note: Lord of the Ōgaki domain, a shogunal-loyalist han renowned for its gunnery ('Ōgaki of the guns'). Being ill, he left the field to his deputy Ohara Tesshin.

小原仁兵衛.note: Deputy commander of the Ōgaki troops, pen-name Tesshin; a noted strategist and student of Western gunnery.

太田市之進.note: A Chōshū samurai of the Saga wing who rallied the wavering Fushimi force at Fujinomori; later known as Mihori Kōsuke.

益田越中.note: A Chōshū elder councillor (karō) commanding the Yamazaki wing of the expedition.

児玉民部.note: A Chōshū commander who led the assault on the Shimodachiuri Gate in the Hamaguri Gate battle.

寺島忠三郎.note: A young Chōshū loyalist, close to Kusaka Genzui, with whom he killed himself at the Takatsukasa mansion when the attack failed.

椿弥十郎.note: The Chōshū samurai who distributed the domain's bill of denunciation against the Aizu lord Matsudaira Katamori.

伊東甲子太郎.note: Born Suzuki Daizō in Hitachi; a Hokushin Ittō-ryū adept and Mito-school loyalist ideologue who kept a dōjō at Fukagawa in Edo. He joined the Shinsengumi at the end of 1864, meaning all along to turn it into a topple-the-shogunate party. His faction would later break away as the Kōdai-ji guardsmen and be destroyed.

尾形俊太郎.note: A jokin of the Shinsengumi and one of its few lettered men, employed by Kondō on documentary and liaison work.

鈴木三樹三郎.note: Itō Kashitarō's younger brother, who joined the corps with him. He later broke away with the Kōdai-ji faction, survived the Restoration, and lived to old age.

篠原泰之進.note: Eldest of Itō's followers, a rōnin of Kurume skilled in both the sword and jūjutsu; the one who warns Itō against trusting his own cleverness. Later a Kōdai-ji guardsman.

加納道之助.note: An old comrade of Itō, later known as Kanō Washio; he went over to the Satsuma side.

服部武雄.note: A man of Bushū and the finest blade among Itō's followers; he died fighting in the Aburanokōji affair.

佐野七五三之助.note: A comrade of Itō who died by his own hand before the Restoration.

中西登.note: A pupil of Itō who later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain.

内海二郎.note: A pupil of Itō who later cast his lot with the Satsuma domain.

松前伊豆守.note: The senior councillor (rōjū) Matsumae Takahiro, whom Kondō claims to have lobbied on the shogun's behalf.

一橋慶喜.note: Tokugawa Yoshinobu (Keiki), head of the Hitotsubashi house and, at this date, Superintendent of the Defense of the Imperial Palace; he became the fifteenth and last shogun in 1866. His personal notice of Kondō marks how high the farmer's son had risen.

上野彦馬.note: A samurai of the Ōmura domain (1838–1904) and a pioneer of photography in Japan, who kept a famous studio at Nagasaki. His portraits of Bakumatsu figures survive; the photograph of Kondō is historical.

松本良順.note: A Dutch-school physician, personal doctor to the shogun Iemochi, who befriended the Shinsengumi and later tended the dying Okita. After the Restoration, as Matsumoto Jun, he became Surgeon-General of the new army and a baron.

千葉周作.note: Historical, 1792/94–1855. Founder of the Hokushin Ittō-ryū and of the Genbukan hall in Edo; his school’s ties to the Mito house made it a seedbed of revere-the-Emperor politics.

武田耕雲斎.note: Historical, 1803–1865. A former chief councillor of the Mito domain who led the Tengu Party’s march on Kyoto and was beheaded, with his family, at Tsuruga. Not to be confused with the Shinsengumi’s Takeda Kanryūsai.

田沼玄蕃頭.note: Tanuma Okitaka (1834–1868), a junior councillor (wakadoshiyori) of the shogunate, grandson of the notorious minister Tanuma Okitsugu. He directed the harsh disposal of the surrendered Tengu Party at Tsuruga.

明里.note: The Shimabara courtesan said to have been Yamanami’s lover. The tradition is famous but late and unverified; see the note at first appearance.

松原忠司.note: Historical Shinsengumi captain of the Fourth Unit, a master of the Sekiguchi school of jūjutsu; died in 1865.

吉村貫一郎.note: Historical inspector of the corps, a Nanbu (Morioka) man; later the subject of Asada Jirō's novel Mibu Gishi Den.

勝海舟.note: Katsu Kaishū (1823–1899), the far-sighted shogunal official who built the first Japanese navy and, in 1868, negotiated the peaceful surrender of Edo Castle.

松平慶永.note: Matsudaira Yoshinaga (Shungaku, 1828–1890), lord of Echizen Fukui, one of the leading reform-minded daimyō of the day and a voice for a union of court and shogunate.

後醍醐天皇.note: The fourteenth-century emperor whose brief Kenmu Restoration (1333) overthrew the Kamakura shogunate; Kusunoki Masashige was his most famous loyal general.

恩智左近.note: A retainer of Kusunoki Masashige, remembered as a loyal lieutenant; Kondō casts Toshizō in the part.

永井主水正尚志.note: Nagai Naomune (1816–1891), a senior shogunal official (here Grand Inspector). Mondo-no-shō is his court title. He led the 1865 embassy that interrogated Chōshū at Hiroshima.

宍戸備後助.note: A borrowed domain-elder’s name under which Chōshū sent a stand-in envoy to the Hiroshima interrogation.

山県半蔵.note: The real name of Chōshū’s sham envoy: Shishido Tamaki (1829–1901), a middle-rank samurai chosen for his glib tongue, after the Restoration a viscount and member of the House of Peers.

レオン・ロッシュ.note: Léon Roches (1809–1900), French minister to Japan 1864–68, who tied France to the shogunate’s cause with loans, arms, and the Yokosuka arsenal.

豊玉.note: Toshizō’s haiku pen-name, known only to his intimates; see ch19.

田中土佐.note: Tanaka Tosa (Genba), a chief retainer of the Aizu domain during its years as Kyoto Protector; he died by his own hand at the fall of Aizu in 1868.

東雲大夫.note: A tayū of the Kizuya house in Shimabara; Toshizō’s partner on the one night the chapter turns on. Dayū is the title of the first rank of courtesan.

米沢藤次.note: A Chōshū samurai and Osae’s lover in Kyoto, through whom she passed shogunate-side intelligence.

鴻池善右衛門.note: The head, by hereditary name, of the Kōnoike house, the greatest merchant-bank of Osaka (see ch15). It bankrolled Kondō in return for the corps’s protection against loyalist extortion.

大谷刑部.note: Ōtani Yoshitsugu (1559–1600), Hideyoshi’s trusted general, renowned for the handling of large forces; see the note here.

藤吉.note: The manservant (komono) attending Toshizō on the rainy night of the ambush.

お雪.cast: The heroine, and the one wholly invented character in the book: an Edo-born samurai widow living alone in Kyoto, a painter, who becomes Toshizō's one love.
お雪.note: Oyuki (given name Yuki) is Shiba’s invention; see the note at her first appearance. She recurs to the end of the novel as the woman who draws out Toshizō’s private self.

加田進次郎.note: Oyuki’s late husband in the novel, an Edo-resident foot-guard of the Ōgaki domain; like Oyuki, a fictional figure.

田中光顕.note: Tanaka Mitsuaki (1843–1939), a Tosa loyalist who after the Restoration became a count and Imperial Household Minister; Shiba quotes his recollection of fearing the Shinsengumi.

吉田良道.note: The Kyoto painter under whom the fictional Oyuki is said to study; part of Shiba’s invented history for her.

小笠原壱岐守.note: Ogasawara Nagamichi (1822–1891), heir of the Karatsu domain and a rōjū of the shogunate, prominent in the Chōshū war and the treaty question; Iki-no-kami is his court title.

西郷吉之助.note: Saigō Takamori (1828–1877), the Satsuma leader — Kichinosuke was his everyday name — a chief architect of the Restoration and, later, of the Meiji state he then rebelled against and died fighting.

広沢兵助.note: Hirosawa Saneomi (1834–1871), a Chōshū official who became a councillor of the Restoration government and was assassinated in 1871; Hyōsuke was an earlier name.

新井忠雄.note: An inspector of the Shinsengumi and one of Itō’s confidants from the Edo days; he left with Itō’s faction.

加納鵰雄.note: A corporal of the Shinsengumi in Itō’s faction; 鵰雄 is a roster variant for the same man written 道之助 elsewhere (see ch27).

中村半次郎.note: Nakamura Hanjirō (1838–1877), later Kirino Toshiaki: a Satsuma swordsman of the Jigen-ryū reckoned one of the ‘four man-cutters’ of the Bakumatsu, close to Saigō Takamori. He rose to general in the imperial army and fell with Saigō at Shiroyama in the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877.

与兵衛.note: The keeper of the night saké-shop that gives the chapter its name.

笠間喜十郎.note: An Echigo rōnin drawn into the ambush; he died of his wound days later, naming Itō as the man behind it.

毛内有之介.note: An inspector of the Shinsengumi (also known by the name Kenmotsu) who left with Itō’s faction.

富山弥兵衛.note: A corporal of the Shinsengumi who went over to Itō’s faction.

大久保一蔵.note: Ōkubo Toshimichi (1830–1878), the Satsuma statesman who, with Saigō and Kido, drove the Restoration and then built the Meiji state; Ichizō was his earlier name. He was assassinated in 1878.

林権助.note: Hayashi Gonsuke (Yasusada), the 63-year-old Aizu commissioner of artillery who commanded the Aizu contingent at Fushimi; killed in the fighting there.

石田村.note: Toshizō's birthplace in the Tama district of Musashi; now part of Hino, Tokyo.

武州多摩.note: The Tama district of Musashi Province (Bushū), the farming country west of Edo; the Shinsengumi's home ground.

府中.note: The old provincial seat of Musashi, on the Kōshū Highway; site of the Ōkunitama Shrine.

八王子.note: A town west of Fuchū on the Kōshū Highway.

甲州街道.note: One of the five great Tokugawa highways, running west from Edo through Fuchū toward Kōfu in Kai (Kōshū).

大国魂神社.note: The head shrine (sōja) of Musashi Province, at Fuchū; also called the Rokusha Myōjin or Rokusho-gū. Its grand festival is the Kurayami (Darkness) Festival.

専修坊.note: The Shinshū temple in Hachiōji of the winter episode. Reading from the source's own furigana; romanization mine.

蕨.note: A post-town just north of Edo, in present-day Saitama; base of the Ryūgō-ryū.

秩父.note: The hill country of western Musashi; home ground of the Kōgen Ittō-ryū.

本所.note: A district on the east bank of the Sumida in Edo.

小石川小日向柳町.note: The Edo neighborhood where Kondō’s training hall (the Shieikan) stood.

上州屋.note: Rihei's inn at the Fuda station on the Kōshū Highway.

布田.note: The central station of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway, in present-day Chōfu.

内藤新宿.note: The first post-station out of Edo on the Kōshū Highway.

上石原.note: A village of the Fuda Five Stations on the Kōshū Highway (now part of Chōfu); Kondō Isami's birthplace.

連雀.note: A village of the Tama country with no fencing hall, where Toshizō taught in the headman's miso storehouse.

小仏峠.note: The pass west of Hachiōji by which the Kōshū Highway crosses into Kai.

千人町.note: The Hachiōji quarter named for the Thousand Guardsmen settled there; site of the Hiruma hall.

馬庭.note: The seat of the Maniwa Nen-ryū in Kōzuke (Jōshū), present-day Gunma.

分倍河原.note: A district on the old Tama-River flats near Fuchū, a road-junction long fought over; site of the 1333 battle and of the duel of this chapter.

分倍橋.note: A small bridge south of Bubaigawara, the appointed place of the fight.

正光院.note: A field-temple with a graveyard near Bubaigawara, where Toshizō sets up his command post.

韮山.note: A seat in Izu of the Egawa house, hereditary shogunal intendants.

伊香保.note: A hot-spring town in Kōzuke (Jōshū), site of the shrine tablet affair between Chiba Shūsaku and the Nen-ryū.

長州.note: The Mōri domain of western Honshū, later the chief power of the anti-shogunal movement and the Shinsengumi's great enemy.

玄武館.note: Chiba Shūsaku's Hokushin Ittō-ryū hall in Edo, greatest of the three great dōjō.

三番町.note: An Edo quarter to which the Saitō hall (Renpeikan) moved after a fire.

壬生.note: A village in the western outskirts of Kyoto, the first quarters and base of the corps that became the Shinsengumi (called, in derision, the Mibu-rō, the ‘Mibu wolves’).

新徳寺.note: The temple at Mibu that served as the Rōshigumi's headquarters, where Kiyokawa revealed his true design.

中仙道.note: The inland highway between Edo and Kyoto, running through the central mountains; longer than the coastal Tōkaidō but free of its river-crossings.

会津.note: The Matsudaira domain of the mountainous northeast, staunchly loyal to the shogunate; its lord was Kyoto Protector and the Shinsengumi's patron, and it fought the Restoration to a bitter end in 1868.

水戸.note: A senior Tokugawa branch domain, and the intellectual seedbed of the revere-the-Emperor school; riven in these years by violent factional strife between its radicals (the Tengu Party) and conservatives.

島原.note: Kyoto’s licensed pleasure quarter, in the southwest of the city; the courtesan district that was to Kyoto what the Yoshiwara was to Edo.

先斗町.note: A narrow lane of teahouses and geisha between the Kamo River and Kiyamachi in central Kyoto.

木屋町.note: The street of taverns and inns along the Takase River; in these years a haunt of loyalist rōnin, backing onto the Chōshū mansion.

高瀬川.note: Not a river but a shallow canal, dug in the early seventeenth century to carry cargo boats (takasebune) between Kyoto and Fushimi; its west bank was lined with the Kyoto mansions of the domains.

角屋.note: A great ageya (house of assignation) in the Shimabara quarter, where guests were entertained by courtesans summoned from the tayū houses; the building survives in Kyoto.

本能寺.note: The Kyoto temple where Oda Nobunaga was destroyed in 1582 by his own general Akechi Mitsuhide; by extension, in Rai San’yō’s poem and in Toshizō’s thought, the place where the true enemy is found to lie.

竹屋町.note: An east–west street in central Kyōto.

二帖半敷町.note: A block in central Kyōto; the crossroads that gives the chapter its name. The name reads literally “two-and-a-half-mat town.”

仏光寺.note: A large Shin-sect temple in central Kyōto; its gate-front was a landmark and a stand for hired palanquins.

宝鏡寺.note: A Rinzai imperial convent (ama-monzeki) in Kyōto whose abbesses were imperial princesses; also called the Momo-no-gosho.

鴨川.note: The river running north to south through the eastern side of Kyōto.

室町.note: A north–south street in central Kyōto.

大仏.note: The colossal Buddha of the Hōkō-ji in Higashiyama, Kyōto’s Daibutsu; “behind the Great Buddha” names the district around it.

本圀寺.note: A temple on Horikawa used as the Kyōto quartering-ground of the Mito clan’s troops.

三条小橋.note: The “little bridge” on Sanjō, over the Takase canal; the Ikedaya stood at its west end.

天竜寺.note: A great Rinzai Zen monastery in Saga, in the western reaches of Kyoto, head temple of its own branch; founded in 1339 to placate the spirit of the late Emperor Go-Daigo. Its walled compound made a natural fortress.

蛤御門.note: The Hamaguri-gomon, the 'Clam Gate,' one of the gates in the wall enclosing the Kyoto Imperial Palace. The battle about to be fought here gave the whole affair its name: the Hamaguri Gate Incident (Kinmon no Hen).

天王山.note: A hill commanding the Yamazaki defile on the road between Kyoto and Osaka, proverbial in Japanese for a decisive position. Maki Izumi and his men made their last stand here.

黒谷.note: The Kurodani precinct (the temple Konkai Kōmyō-ji), on the eastern hills of Kyoto, which served as the Aizu domain's Kyoto headquarters.

三田尻.note: Chōshū's chief port on the Inland Sea, in Suō province (the modern Hōfu), from which the domain shipped its expeditionary force toward Osaka.

護王神社.note: A shrine facing the west side of the Kyoto Imperial Palace, dedicated to Wake no Kiyomaro; a landmark on the line of the Chōshū advance.

筋違橋.note: A bridge on the road north of Fujinomori, where the Ōgaki troops caught the Chōshū column crossing.

藤ノ森.note: The district and shrine (Fujinomori-myōjin) south of Kyoto, on the Daibutsu highroad, where the Fushimi fighting opened.

鷹司屋敷.note: The Kyoto residence of the Takatsukasa regental house, on the palace's edge, where Kusaka Genzui and Terashima Chūzaburō died.

興正寺.note: A monzeki (imperially-connected) temple in Kyoto, next to the Nishi-Honganji; Kondō kept a rest-lodging at its lower villa.

敦賀.note: A port town on the Sea of Japan, in Echizen (modern Fukui), where the Tengu Party was imprisoned and executed.

越前.note: The old province along the Sea of Japan north of Lake Biwa, modern Fukui.

加賀.note: The great domain on the Sea of Japan (modern Ishikawa), held by the Maeda house; its levy took the Tengu Party’s surrender.

来迎寺.note: A temple at the edge of Tsuruga; the mass beheadings of the Tengu Party were carried out in its grounds.

筑波山.note: The twin-peaked mountain of Hitachi, long a sacred site, where the Tengu Party first rose in 1864.

常州.note: An old name (read Jōshū) for Hitachi Province, the Mito country northeast of Edo; rendered ‘Hitachi’ here to keep it distinct from Jōshū = Kōzuke, another province of the same reading.

大津.note: The first post-town east of Kyoto on the Tōkaidō, on the south shore of Lake Biwa.

前川屋敷.note: One of the requisitioned residences at Mibu that served as Shinsengumi barracks; Yamanami was confined and died here.

姫路.note: The castle town of Banshū (Harima), west of Osaka.

大垣.note: A fudai castle-town and domain in Mino (modern Gifu), ‘Ōgaki of the guns’ (see ch25).

十津川.note: A mountain district of Yamato (modern Nara) whose rural samurai were fierce imperial loyalists; see the note here.

桑名.note: A fudai domain in Ise, held by a branch of the Matsudaira; with Aizu it stood staunchly for the shogunate to the end.

唐津.note: A domain in Hizen, in northwest Kyushu; Ogasawara was its daimyō’s heir.

馬関.note: The old name for the strait and port at Shimonoseki, the western mouth of the Inland Sea, in Chōshū territory.

泉涌寺.note: An ancient temple in Kyoto’s Higashiyama, mortuary temple of the imperial house.

戒光寺.note: A sub-temple within the grounds of Sennyū-ji, where Itō’s faction met.

高幡不動.note: A temple of Fudō Myō-ō in the Tama country of Bushū, near Hijikata’s home village of Ishida; the family kept ties to it.

花昌町.note: The site of the Shinsengumi’s last Kyoto barracks (also called Fudōdō-mura), near Samegai, Shichijō, and the Horikawa; no such place-name survives today. The source glosses the name kashō-chō.

高台寺.note: A temple in Kyoto’s Higashiyama; the Goryō-eji fixed their headquarters at its sub-temple Gettsuin, whence they were also called the Kōdai-ji party.

月真院.note: A sub-temple of Kōdai-ji; the Goryō-eji made it their headquarters, whence they were called the Kōdai-ji party.

御香宮.note: The Gokō-no-miya shrine at Fushimi; its wooded precinct became the Satsuma army's forward post in 1868, directly north of the Magistracy.

新選組.note: The 'Newly Selected Corps,' the shogunate's Kyoto police militia of swordsmen, 1863–1869; the subject of the novel.

天然理心流.note: The country school of swordsmanship, founded by Kondō Kuranosuke and headed in this book by Kondō Isami; the school of Hijikata, Okita, and the Tama men. Known for overwhelming an opponent’s spirit and for close, practical fighting rather than polish.

甲源一刀流.note: A sword school of the Chichibu country, founded 1776 by Henmi Tashirō; the school of Rokusha Sōhaku and, along the Kōshū Highway, the chief rival of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

柳剛流.note: A school founded by Okada Sōemon, based at Warabi, notorious for shin-cutting strikes and for teaching the glaive alongside the sword.

北辰一刀流.note: The great Edo sword school of Chiba Shūsaku, at the height of its fame in these years; Tōdō Heisuke’s school.

神道無念流.note: A widely practiced Edo sword school; Nagakura Shinpachi held its full transmission.

荒木流.note: A composite martial school of Kōzuke, taught iai among other arts; Shichiri Kennosuke's iai line.

念流.note: Here the Maniwa Nen-ryū of Kōzuke, one of the oldest surviving sword schools; where Shichiri first trained.

浪士組.note: The ‘corps of masterless men,’ levied by the shogunate in 1863 to go up to Kyoto ostensibly as the shogun's guard. Split by Kiyokawa's imperial gambit; the remnant that stayed in Kyoto became the Shinsengumi.

天狗党.note: The radical revere-the-Emperor faction of the Mito domain, which in 1864 rose in open revolt and was crushed.

京都守護職.note: The shogunal office created in 1862 to keep order in Kyoto, held by Matsudaira Katamori of Aizu; the Shinsengumi served under its authority.

学習院.note: Not the later peers’ school of the same name but a court institution of 1863: a hall within the Imperial Palace where sympathetic nobles met loyalist activists to debate policy toward the shogunate.

新徴組.note: The “Newly Levied Corps.” The rōnin who followed Kiyokawa back to Edo were reorganized under this name and set, under the Shōnai domain, to police the city; the corps lasted to the end of the shogunate.

鴻池.note: The greatest merchant-and-banking house of Osaka, financiers to daimyo and shogunate alike.

所司代.note: The Kyoto Deputy, the shogunate’s standing office for the government and policing of the capital, older and more regular than the Kyoto Protector under whom the Shinsengumi served.

芳駕籠.note: The palanquin-house by the Bukkō-ji gate. Apparently the novelist’s invention.

見廻組.note: The Kyōto Mimawarigumi, a patrol corps like the Shinsengumi but manned by direct shogunal retainers (hatamoto and gokenin), and so of higher formal standing.

枡屋.note: The tool-and-sundries shop that was the front for Furutaka’s arms depot.

茨木屋.note: The sundries-wholesaler on Kawaramachi from whose upper floor the corps kept watch on the Masuya.

丹虎.note: A Kiyamachi restaurant kept by Shikokuya Jūbei, the second suspected meeting-place; the object of Toshizō’s party on the night of the raid.

池田屋.note: The inn at the west end of Sanjō-kobashi, kept by one Sōbei, where the loyalists met and where Kondō’s party struck.

御陵衛士.note: ‘Guards of the Imperial Tomb’: the loyalist band Itō formed on breaking with the Shinsengumi in 1867, given the charge of tending Emperor Kōmei’s grave at Sennyū-ji.

石田散薬.note: The Hijikata family's patent remedy for bruises and broken bones, made and peddled from the early eighteenth century until 1948.

里.note: A unit of distance, about 3.9 km (2.4 miles).

名主.note: The headman of a village, lowest office of Tokugawa rural administration: a leading farmer, not a samurai.

旗本.note: A direct bannerman of the shogun, with the right of audience; a samurai of the Tokugawa house itself, ranked above the ordinary domain retainer.

居合.note: The art of drawing the sword and cutting in a single motion; a specialty distinct from ordinary fencing.

代官.note: A shogunal officer administering a district of the Tokugawa house's own lands in place of a resident lord.

衢地.note: From Sunzi's Art of War: a place where the roads of several regions meet, from which armies are readily moved.

気組.note: The marshalling of spirit to overwhelm an opponent; the watchword of the Tennen Rishin-ryū.

太平記.note: The fourteenth-century war-chronicle of the wars of the Northern and Southern Courts, a storytellers' staple.

猿田彦.note: The guiding deity of Japanese myth, shown as a long-nosed, red-faced figure; his mask (rubied here in the source as Sarudahiko) was one of those the waiwai-tennō wore.

牛頭天王.note: The 'Ox-Head Heavenly King,' plague-warding deity of the Gion and Tennō shrines, whose talismans the waiwai-tennō sold.

尊皇攘夷.note: The rallying slogan of the late-shogunate loyalists: reverence for the Emperor joined to the demand that the foreigner be driven out. Its logic pointed, in the end, past the shogunate itself.

講武所.note: The shogunate's own military academy in Edo, opened in 1856 to modernize the training of its retainers in swordsmanship, gunnery, and Western arms.

辻斬り.note: ‘Crossroads-cutting’: the testing of a blade, or of one's nerve, by cutting down a stranger on the road at night. Long a capital crime, it revived in the murderous mood of these years.

鉄扇.note: A folding fan with iron ribs (or a solid iron bar shaped like one), carried where a sword might give offense and used to parry or strike.

公用方.note: A domain's political-liaison bureau, handling its dealings with the court, the shogunate, and other domains in Kyoto.

和泉守兼定.note: A celebrated sword-signature. The blade Hijikata carried through his life bore it; see the note at its first appearance.

虎徹.note: The prized blades of the Edo smith Nagasone Kotetsu. Kondō's famous ‘Kotetsu’ was, by most accounts, a forgery; see the note where he hunts for one.

局長.note: Kyokuchō, the title of a corps-captain in the Shinsengumi; three were made at the founding, to balance the Serizawa and Kondō lines.

副長.note: Fukuchō, second to the commander; Hijikata’s chosen post, from which he worked the corps.

助勤.note: A line officer of the corps, adjutant in quarters and platoon-leader in the field; the term borrowed from the student self-government of the shōgunal college.

監察.note: Kansatsu, the corps’s internal watch and intelligence officers, answering to the vice-commander.

士道.note: Shidō, the way of the warrior; the governing idea of the corps, and of this chapter. In the Shinsengumi it hardened into a written code whose central charge, “failure in the warrior’s code,” carried death.

局中法度.note: The written law of the Shinsengumi, breach of it punishable by seppuku. See the note in the chapter on its debated historicity.

日本外史.note: Rai San’yō’s Unofficial History of Japan (1827), the stirring, imperial-centered history that did as much as any book to shape the loyalist feeling of the age. See ch12.

堀川国広.note: A short-sword of the Kyoto smith Horikawa Kunihiro (c.1531–1614); Toshizō’s companion blade to the long Izumi-no-kami Kanesada (see ch12, ch17).

王政復古.note: The Ōsei Fukko coup of Keiō 3/12/9 (3 January 1868): the shogunate and regency abolished, direct Imperial rule declared.
